ch05.note: “Sima Road” means “Fourth Horse Road.” The east–west streets of the International Settlement were known in Chinese by number as malu, “horse roads”: First (today Nanjing East Road), Second (Jiujiang Road), Third or Sanma Road (today Hankou Road), Fourth or Sima Road (today Fuzhou Road), Fifth (Guangdong Road). Fourth Horse Road was famous for its bookshops and teahouses, its theaters and its brothels alike.

Xiong Jinding (1886–1973), the “Red Boss,” managed the underground Party’s money in Shanghai from 1928 and, with Zhu Duanshou, kept the Yunnan Road safe house that doubled as the Politburo’s meeting place. He came through the underground years, held finance and united-front posts after 1949, and is the central figure of this chapter. Corroborated across the Party-history literature.

The Shanghai Race Club’s course (the paomating), a great grandstand and turf oval that the British ran in the heart of the settlement, at the west end of Fourth Horse Road; the grounds are today People’s Park and People’s Square.

ch05.anchor: a solid shop to stand surety
ch05.note: To rent property in Shanghai one commonly needed a pubao—a going concern of known standing willing to vouch for the tenant and answer for the rent. A stranger with no local ties could not readily produce one. This is the author’s point against the romantic “found it by chance in the rain” version: a safe house was hard to secure, and the finding of it was the First Section’s trade, not a lone accountant’s luck.

The betrayal recounted in Chapter Three: in 1928 He Jiaxing and his wife He Zhihua gave up Luo Yinong, a member of the Politburo Standing Committee, to the concession police, and he was shot. Here the author invokes it to show how wary landlords were of tenants who spoke the wrong dialect.

Nan Hanchen (1895–1967) was the first governor of the People’s Bank of China, founded in 1949, and later chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade; an old hand at the Party’s underground finance, which is why the Xiongs’ appeal came to his desk.

Xiong Xiaosan was a Nationalist general and Xiong Jinding’s son by an earlier marriage; father and son took opposite sides after 1927. Zhou Enlai’s statement records that he received his father’s letter urging him to come over during the Huaihai Campaign (1948–49) but held out, and fled when the Communists attacked.

From a couplet Xiong Jinding wrote in old age (the 1987 date is that of the source that prints it). “Fish and water” (yushui) is the stock Chinese figure for a perfect, inseparable union, of ruler and minister or of husband and wife; the line sums up his four decades and more with Zhu Duanshou.

Wuhao was Zhou Enlai’s best-known cover name in the underground years. It was later turned against him: in 1932 the Nationalists planted a forged notice, the so-called “Wuhao renouncing the Party” announcement, over his alias—a slander revived to attack him in the Cultural Revolution.

A wash of alum dissolved in water was a standard developer for invisible ink: a message written in a colorless solution and dried would come up again when brushed over with the alum wash. The Special Branch used it on documents sent up from the soviet areas.

Chao bazi, literally “going through the target,” was Shanghai slang for the concession police’s snap body-searches in the street or at a checkpoint—the standing hazard for a courier carrying documents on their person.

Zhibu Shenghuo, an internal bulletin of the Party’s central-organs branch, edited by Deng Yingchao, Zhou Enlai’s wife. A print run of seventy-five copies gives the measure of how small and closed the underground apparatus was.

A play on sound: the branch’s abbreviation (zhizhi, “directly subordinate”) and its codename (zhizhi, “plant a branch”) are homophones written with different characters—a small piece of underground wordcraft.

In the shikumen lanes, which had no plumbing, each household’s night-soil bucket (matong) was carried out at dawn to be emptied at the lane’s collection point and scrubbed in the street—women’s work by custom. The debate Zhu Duanshou relished turned a chamber pot into a question of the sexes’ equality; Zhou Enlai’s counter was that a household that broke the custom would catch a watcher’s eye.

Hongshao shizitou, “red-cooked lion’s heads”—oversized pork meatballs braised until meltingly soft, a signature of Huaiyang cooking from the lower Yangtze. The name likens the big meatball, ringed with cabbage, to a lion’s maned head; the dish gives the section its title.

ch05.anchor: Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Teng
ch05.note: Wang Bo (c. 650–676), a prodigy of the early Tang, wrote this celebrated rhapsody. The line Xiong Jinding read out—“The setting glow and a lone wild duck fly as one; the autumn waters and the boundless sky are of a single hue”—is among the most famous in all of Chinese parallel prose.

Bai Juyi (772–846), one of the great Tang poets; his Chang hen ge tells of the Xuanzong emperor’s doomed love for the consort Yang Guifei. Its closing couplet, which Xiong quoted—“Heaven is lasting and earth enduring, yet a time will come when both are gone; but this regret runs on and on, and will never reach an end”—is proverbial. Song of the Pipa is another of Bai’s long narrative poems.

Classical ci lyrics were composed to fixed metrical patterns, each named for a “tune-title” (cipai) that fixed the number and length of the lines and the placing of the rhymes. So “Southern Song,” “Fisherman’s Song,” “Partridge Sky,” and “Recalling the Maid of Qin” are verse forms, not subjects.

ch05.anchor: a traitor risen within the Party
ch05.note: Gu Shunzhang, who ran the Special Branch’s own operations and knew its every secret, defected to the Nationalists in April 1931 and forced the Party to abandon its Shanghai premises overnight—the disaster that closed the Yunnan Road safe house. His betrayal and its aftermath fill later chapters.
Yuan Mei (1716–1798), a leading poet and essayist of the Qing, known for verse of feeling and spontaneity and for holding that a poem should speak the writer’s own nature.

The West Hunan–Hubei (Xiang–E–Xi) Soviet base, on the lakes and marshes around Honghu, was built by He Long from 1928; it fell to the Nationalists’ “encirclement and suppression” campaigns in 1932. Xiong Jinding and Zhu Duanshou were posted there when the Shanghai organ closed.

ch05.anchor: the Zhou residence on Rue Massenet
ch05.note: In 1946 Zhou Enlai led the Communist delegation in Shanghai during the failing Nationalist–Communist negotiations; his residence and office at 107 Rue Massenet (today 73 Sinan Road) is preserved as the “Zhou Residence” museum.

ch05.anchor: Fourth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee in January 1931
ch05.note: The Fourth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee (January 1931), at which the Moscow-trained group around Wang Ming took hold of the Party. Here it serves only to date how long the Yunnan Road organ went undetected—more than two years.

ch05.anchor: Wu Jieping brought in to treat him as well
ch05.note: Wu Jieping (1917–2011), a renowned urologist who attended many of the Party’s leaders; that Zhou Enlai sent him marks the regard in which the dying Xiong Jinding was held.

The “Gang of Four”—Jiang Qing (Mao’s wife), Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen—were the radical leaders who drove the Cultural Revolution and, in its last years, worked against the ailing Zhou Enlai. They were arrested a month after Mao’s death in 1976.

The “Horse Day” Incident of May 21, 1927: ma, “horse,” was the telegraph code for the twenty-first of the month. Nationalist officers in Changsha crushed the Communist-led peasant and labor unions in a bloody purge—one of the opening blows of the 1927 terror, and the moment that drove many Hunan revolutionaries, Xiong and Zhu among them, underground.

Shili yangchang, “the ten-li foreign market,” was the stock epithet for Shanghai’s foreign concessions—ten li of gaslit, moneyed, half-Western streets that stood for the whole glittering and treacherous city.

The detail is the source's and is faithful: in traditional Chinese medicine, repeated yawning is read as an early sign of a chill (zhaoliang), a symptom of the body's yang being caught off guard. Xiong Jinding, trained in Chinese medicine, takes his own yawning for proof he has caught cold and so has a pretext to register as a patient.

ch05.anchor: Xiong Changsu, daughter of Xiong Jinding
ch05.note: Xiong Changsu, daughter of the underground financier Xiong Jinding and Zhu Duanshou, is the chapter’s chief living witness; the author draws throughout on her recollections and on her mother’s autobiography, which she preserved.

ch05.anchor: Zhou Enlai's niece Zhou Bingde and nephew Zhou Bingjun
ch05.note: Zhou Bingjun, a nephew of Zhou Enlai, was among the children and grandchildren of early Party leaders who gathered at the Yunnan Road site in June 2009 (romanization provisional).
Liu Aiqin was a daughter of Liu Shaoqi (1898–1969), a top CCP leader who later became head of state of the People’s Republic before dying in disgrace during the Cultural Revolution.
Wo Baotian was the husband of Liu Aiqin (romanization provisional).
Chen Weihua was a daughter of Chen Yun (1905–1995), one of the Party’s most senior leaders and the chief architect of its economic policy for much of the PRC era.

ch05.anchor: Bo Gu (Qin Bangxian)'s son Qin Tie
ch05.note: Qin Tie was a son of Bo Gu, Party name of Qin Bangxian (1907–1946), one of the Moscow-trained students who led the CCP in the early 1930s (romanization provisional).
Kai Feng (1906–1955) was the Party name of He Kequan, a CCP propaganda leader associated with the returned-student group of the early 1930s; his son He Ming was among the 2009 visitors.
He Kequan was better known by his Party name, Kai Feng (1906–1955), a leading figure in CCP propaganda work.
Pan Guanru was a nephew of Pan Hannian (1906–1977), the celebrated Communist intelligence officer of the Shanghai underground (romanization provisional).

ch05.anchor: Shengli Hospital at No. 447 Yunnan Road
ch05.note: The Shengli Hospital was a small clinic occupying the ground floor of No. 447 Yunnan Road; the Party’s secret premises, known outwardly as the “Fuxing” firm, were the three rooms on the floor above, screened by the clinic below. The author later notes the clinic in fact specialized in venereal disease.

Gong Yinbing (1900–1976) was a lifelong underground Party financier and Xiong Jinding’s predecessor as the Center’s chief accountant in Shanghai; he handed the post over on leaving to attend the Sixth Congress in Moscow in 1928.
Tang Liang (1910–1986) was a People’s Liberation Army general; the 1956 testimonial quoted here was written by Gong Yinbing to vouch for him.

Gong Yuzhi (1929–2007), Gong Yinbing’s son, was a Party historian and theorist who rose to deputy head of the Central Propaganda Department; he is quoted on how little his father, like other underground workers, ever said of his past.

Xie Xiaonai, author of A Devoted Heart (1986), was an early biographer of Xiong Jinding; the author treats his account of how the Yunnan Road organ was set up with skepticism (romanization provisional).

The Tianchan Stage was a famous Peking-opera theater on Sima Road (Fourth Horse Road); the Party’s secret premises stood in an inconspicuous alley behind it. The building survives today as the Labor Theater.

Taichenli was a lane off Avenue Joffre, the grand thoroughfare of the French Concession (today Huaihai Middle Road); this and the addresses that follow trace the moves of the family He Long left behind in Shanghai (romanization provisional).
Kangti Road was a street in the French Concession; its French name is uncertain and the form is kept as pinyin.
Ximen Road was a French Concession street, today Zizhong Road.
Shenchengli was a lane compound in the French Concession where He Long’s family lodged.
Rue Ratard was a street in the French Concession, today Julu Road.
Meishouli was a Shanghai lane compound, the last of the several addresses named here for He Long’s family (romanization provisional).

The Hunan Guild Hall in Hankou was a native-place association (huiguan) — a lodging and mutual-aid house maintained for sojourners from a common home province, here Hunan. Zhu Duanshou boarded there and so came to know Xiong Jinding better.

The Taolechun was a Sichuan restaurant on Sima Road (Fourth Horse Road); it was here, at the Mid-Autumn Festival of 1928, that Zhou Enlai proposed the match that turned Xiong Jinding and Zhu Duanshou’s cover marriage into a real one.

Gengwu was the eldest daughter of Xiong Jinding and Zhu Duanshou. Injured as an infant when patrolmen slammed her head against the floor during the 1933 raid, she suffered lasting ill health and died of heart disease in 1961, aged thirty-one (romanization provisional).
Sangyu was the couple’s third daughter, who took pneumonia at half a year and died in infancy for want of medicine (romanization provisional).
Liwu was the couple’s fifth child, born in 1945; the child later died young of diphtheria (romanization provisional).
Northwest Shanxi (Jinxibei) was a Communist base area in the mountainous northwest of Shanxi province, held through the war against Japan and the civil war that followed.

The Shanxi–Chahar–Hebei (Jin–Cha–Ji) border region was a major Communist base area straddling those three provinces — Chahar being a since-abolished province of the northern frontier — and one of the war years’ model administrations behind Japanese lines.
Zhu Baosan Road was a Shanghai street named for Zhu Baosan (1848–1926), a prominent Ningbo-born merchant and civic figure of the treaty-port era; it is today Xikou Road.

ch06.note: Tu Zuochao (1903–1988), a Hunan carpenter who trained as a wireless mechanic in the Soviet Union and became one of the Party’s first radio technicians; his codename “Carpenter” came from his boyhood trade. The chapter title, “It Was Not Me, It Was the Wind,” plays on the book’s conceit for radio work — the Communists as “windtalkers” who chase, listen for, and catch the wind of the airwaves. Corroborated in the Party-history literature.

Sandaotou, literally “three stripes,” was Shanghai slang for the patrolmen of the French Concession police, after the three braids or chevrons on their sleeves. The “tiger skin” a line later is the uniform itself: a stock image for borrowed official authority, as a lesser beast might dress in a tiger’s hide.

Yangjingbang English, named for a filled-in creek that once divided the foreign settlements, was the improvised trade-English of the Shanghai waterfront — a mix of English words, Chinese grammar, and coinages that outsiders found hard to follow. Here it is part of the painter’s disguise.

The Sixth National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party met from June to July 1928 outside Moscow — the only Party congress held abroad. After the Nationalist purges of 1927 no venue in China was safe, so delegates were smuggled to the Soviet Union. It is the setting in which several figures of this chapter first crossed paths.

ch06.anchor: Moscow's University of the East struck Tu Zuochao
ch06.note: The Communist University of the Toilers of the East (KUTV), founded in Moscow in 1921 to train revolutionaries from Asia; many early CCP cadres passed through it. The “International Wireless Training Class” mentioned here was one of its technical courses.

The Cheka (from the Russian initials for the “Extraordinary Commission”) was the Soviet political police founded in 1917; by 1929 its functions had passed to the OGPU, but the old name stuck in common speech. The station at Vladivostok served the Soviet Far East.

ch06.anchor: came to the revolution through New Youth
ch06.note: New Youth (Xin Qingnian, also published under the French title La Jeunesse), edited by Chen Duxiu, was the seminal magazine of the New Culture and May Fourth movements from 1915; it carried the first Chinese expositions of Marxism and drew a generation, Li Qiang among them, toward the Party.

Lord Mengchang (died 279 BCE), a noble of the Warring States kingdom of Qi, was famous for keeping some three thousand retainers of every description and standing by them; his name became a byword for open-handed, risk-taking patronage. Xia Yan means that Cai Shuhou sheltered the hunted as such a patron would.

The “4-12” is the coup of April 12, 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek’s forces, with Green Gang gunmen, turned on their Communist allies in Shanghai and massacred them — the event that opened the White Terror and drove the Party underground.

Xia Yan (1900–1995), pen name of Shen Naixi, was a leading left-wing playwright, screenwriter, and journalist, later a vice-minister of culture in the People’s Republic. His memoir Lazily Seeking Old Dreams is a standard source on the Shanghai underground’s cultural world.

An illuminated news display — letters spelled out by rows of electric bulbs and run in sequence — mounted on the roof of the Great World amusement arcade, an early piece of Shanghai’s electric spectacle.

The “Hao cipher” (Haomi) took its name from Zhou Enlai’s Party codename Wuhao. It combined transposition of the Chinese commercial telegraph code with a letter-to-figure substitution, was never reused, and was reckoned all but unbreakable; the Nationalists are said never to have read it. Deng Yingchao, Zhou’s wife, was its first cipher clerk.

The observatory at Xujiahui — known in the Republican period by its older French-Jesuit name, Zikawei — was founded by Jesuits in 1872 and was the great weather and time-signal station of the China coast; its forecasts, broadcast on long wave, were what Zhang Shenchuan practiced copying.

Two tortures of the period. On the “tiger bench” (laohudeng) the victim was tied seated with legs held flat while bricks were forced under the ankles, bending the knees backward to breaking. The “duckling’s paddle” (ya’er fushui) was a form of forced near-drowning. Both were standard in Nationalist police cells.

ch06.anchor: in the shape of the Eight Trigrams
ch06.note: The Eight Trigrams (bagua) are the eight three-line figures of the Book of Changes, traditionally arranged in a ring. The prison’s radial plan set nine cell-blocks around a central watch-pavilion, so that a few guards could oversee every corridor — a Chinese cousin of the panopticon. The blocks were named for the trigrams and the virtues: Heaven, Earth, Man, Sun, Moon, Star, Wisdom, Benevolence, Courage.

Yun Daiying (1895–1931), a founder of the Socialist Youth League and one of the Party’s most beloved teachers of the young, was arrested in 1930 and, once Gu Shunzhang’s defection exposed him, executed at the Central Military Prison in April 1931 at thirty-six. His prison quatrain, quoted here, circulated widely among the inmates. Corroborated.

“Captive of Chu” (Chu qiu) alludes to Zhong Yi, a musician of Chu held prisoner in Jin who kept his home dress and home music and never bent, recorded in the Zuo Zhuan; it came to mean a captive who keeps his dignity and his loyalties intact. Yun Daiying casts himself so.

Labor University (Laoda), founded at Jiangwan in 1927, tried to fuse study with manual work in the spirit of the worker-study movement, and carried a strong anarchist strain; its patrons included the KMT elders Cai Yuanpei, Wu Zhihui, Li Shizeng, and Zhang Jingjiang. It was closed in 1932.

Zhou Libo (1908–1979) became one of the People’s Republic’s most celebrated novelists; his land-reform novel The Hurricane won a Stalin Prize, and Great Changes in a Mountain Village chronicled collectivization. Here he is a fellow student expelled with Su Gangda.

Liu Renjing (1902–1987) was one of the dozen or so delegates to the Party’s founding First Congress in 1921 and first head of its youth league; he later became a Trotskyist, which is why he is among the “penitents” here rather than in the Party’s pantheon.

Cao Diqiu (1909–1976) rose after 1949 to be mayor of Shanghai; he was hounded to his death during the Cultural Revolution. The parenthetical string of names and dates in this passage is the author’s own roll-call of the notables the Reformatory happened to hold.

Liao Zhongkai (1877–1925) was the left-Nationalist leader and financier of the first KMT–CCP alliance, assassinated in 1925. His son-in-law Li Shaoshi worked in the underground and was shot dead in Chongqing in 1945 in a still-disputed incident.

“Granny Xia,” Huang Youmei (1870–1944), was the mother-in-law of the martyr Zhao Shiyan (executed 1927) and mother of Xia Zhixu; she sheltered underground workers for years and was honored in the Party’s memory as a “revolutionary mother.”

Both went on to eminence in the arts: Zhang Ding (1917–2010) as a designer and painter who helped shape the national emblem and much official art, Ling Zifeng (1917–1999) as a leading film director. In 1936 they were young men in the Reformatory.

ch06.anchor: sham CCP general secretary Xiang Zhongfa
ch06.note: Xiang Zhongfa (1880–1931) was the Party’s general secretary until his arrest and quick capitulation in June 1931; his story fills a later chapter. The word “sham” (wei) and the framing are the Nationalist booklet’s own; the author quotes them as evidence of what the “penitents” were made to read.

ch06.anchor: the Three Principles of the People
ch06.note: The Three Principles of the People (Sanmin zhuyi) — nationalism, democracy, and the people’s livelihood — were Sun Yat-sen’s doctrine and the official creed of the Nationalist state; to “propagate doctrines incompatible with” them was the standing charge against Communists.

Two of these names differ from the school’s own roster given earlier, where the same trainees appear as Feng Yiping and He Shida. The divergence is in the sources — the newspaper worked from police-blotter names, themselves partly the prisoners’ false confessions — and is left as printed.

Su Gangda’s little verse of paired four-character lines doubles as a coded farewell to smuggle out to his family: its last line, gaowei qinren, mingtian zaijian — “give comfort to your kin; till we meet again tomorrow” — supplies this section’s title and reads, in the mouth of a condemned man, as a promise past death.

ch06.anchor: Sixteen trainees in all gathered at the Welfare Electric Company
ch06.note: The author's headcounts for the training school do not quite square, and are reproduced as printed. Sixteen trainees are named here as the full enrollment; the raid scene below counts “eighteen trainees” present that afternoon; and the arrest tallies run to “the other twenty” and to seventeen-plus-three sentenced — figures that evidently fold in the instructors (Zhang Shenchuan, Zeng Hualun, Fang Tingzhen and others) and any who joined the class after this roll was taken. The discrepancy is the source's, not a slip of translation.

The conceit turns on feng (“wind”) for the airwaves: the radio men chase, listen for, and catch the wind. The Chinese word rendered “windtalkers,” fengyuzhe, is also the Chinese title of the 2002 war film Windtalkers, about the Navajo code-talkers of the Pacific war; the author is punning on it. No connection to the Navajo cipher is implied.

ch07.anchor: first proposed at the National Congress of Soviet Areas
ch07.note: The National Congress of Soviet Areas (全国苏维埃区域代表大会) gathered delegates from the Communist base areas and the Red Army in Shanghai in the spring of 1930. It resolved to convene a First National Soviet Congress, which duly met at Ruijin in November 1931 and founded the Chinese Soviet Republic. The event is well attested; its exact dates are not (see the note at “May 5, 1930”).
In Ding Ling’s original the Communist Party could not be named in print under the censorship of the day, so it appears as “××.” The blanks stand for the Communist Party.

ch07.anchor: the writer Ding Ling in her
ch07.note: Ding Ling (1904–1986), one of the foremost women writers of the century and later a leading literary figure of the People’s Republic; her documentary sketch “Shanghai, Spring 1930” appeared that same year. Her husband, the writer Hu Yepin, is a subject of this chapter.

ch07.anchor: Xiong Shihui read over and over the words plainly set down there
ch07.note: Xiong Shihui (1893–1974), a Kuomintang general; at this time commander of the Shanghai–Wusong garrison and thus the “commander” of the chapter, later governor of Jiangxi. It was in that capacity that he directed the hunt for the congress.

ch07.anchor: assigned by Zhou Enlai as an assistant to the famous Soviet spy Sorge
ch07.note: Richard Sorge (1895–1944), the Soviet Union’s master intelligence agent in the Far East, who ran a network in Shanghai and later Tokyo; he was arrested in Japan in 1941 and hanged in 1944. Zhang Wenqiu’s claim to have assisted him is her own and is debated by historians. Her two daughters, Liu Siqi and Shaohua, married Mao Zedong’s sons Mao Anying and Mao Anqing — hence “Mao Zedong’s kinswoman by marriage.” The same Sorge network reappears at the chapter’s end through Ozaki Hotsumi.

ch07.anchor: was an alias used by Deng Fa in September 1937
ch07.note: Deng Fa (1906–1946), a Communist labor leader and, later, security chief; he died in the same 1946 plane crash as Ye Ting and Wang Ruofei. Here the author is weighing his sources: if “Fang Lin” really was Deng Fa, the dates do not fit, since in early 1930 Deng Fa held only provincial posts in Guangdong and Hong Kong and was in a Hong Kong jail. The identification is doubtful.

ch07.anchor: his own spear against his own shield
ch07.note: From the parable in the Han Feizi of the peddler who boasted at once of a shield nothing could pierce and a spear that would pierce anything, until a bystander asked what would happen if the one met the other. The Chinese word for “contradiction,” maodun, is literally “spear-shield.” The sense here is turning the enemy’s own ground and methods against him.

ch07.anchor: the great hermit who hides in the city
ch07.note: From a poem by the Jin-dynasty writer Wang Kangju: “The lesser hermit hides in the hills and marshes; the great hermit hides in the court and market.” True concealment is not flight to the wilderness but invisibility in the thick of the crowd — the conceit of the chapter’s title.

ch07.anchor: on Hart Road in the British Concession
ch07.note: Shanghai had no “British Concession”: the British and American settlements had merged in 1863 into the jointly administered International Settlement. The memoir sources loosely call it the “British Concession” because the Settlement was British-dominated. Hart Road lay in the Settlement’s western district, which is the author’s correction in the paragraph that follows.

A stock phrase for a warren of a tenement crammed with poor households of every trade and temper, made proverbial by the comic play and film The Seventy-Two Tenants. The number is figurative, meaning “a great many.”

Zhao Yiman (1905–1936), born Li Kuntai, an organizer and commander of the anti-Japanese resistance in Manchuria. Captured wounded in November 1935, she endured months of torture and was executed by the Japanese near Zhuhe (today Shangzhi, Heilongjiang) in August 1936. Her farewell letter to her young son, quoted here, is among the best-known texts of the resistance; the 1950 film Zhao Yiman made her a household name. Well attested.

The Mauser C96, the broom-handled semi-automatic pistol that the Chinese called the “box cannon” (hezipao); with its detachable wooden holster-stock it was the favored sidearm of the Special Branch’s action men.

ch07.anchor: the concessions' Municipal Council and French Municipal Council
ch07.note: The two concession governments: the Shanghai Municipal Council (gongbuju), which ran the International Settlement, and the French Municipal Council (gongdongju), which ran the French Concession. Each kept its own police, courts, and prisons.

ch07.anchor: was a product of Li Lisan's
ch07.note: The “Li Lisan line” was the ultra-left course that briefly dominated the Party in mid-1930, ordering armed uprisings in the great cities on the belief that a nationwide revolutionary high tide was at hand. It was checked at the enlarged Third Plenum in September 1930 and repudiated soon after. Li Lisan himself long outlived it.

ch07.anchor: Red May drew nearer by the day
ch07.note: “Red May” (hong wuyue) was the revolutionary calendar’s crowded month of commemorations — May Day and the memorial days of the movement’s dead — a season of heightened Communist activity and, in answer, heightened repression.

The earliest Chinese Communist flags bore a crossed sickle and axe (lian-dao fu-tou), the axe standing for the industrial worker; the design was later standardized as the sickle and hammer of the international movement.

ch07.anchor: I told Ozaki about it and asked him to help
ch07.note: Ozaki Hotsumi (1901–1944), correspondent of the Asahi Shimbun and a noted authority on China, sympathetic to the Communist cause. He was a key member of Richard Sorge’s Soviet spy ring; arrested in 1941, he was hanged in 1944, the same year as Sorge. The two men’s appearance at either end of this chapter — Sorge above, Ozaki here — is a genuine crossing of the threads.

ch07.anchor: At about nine on the morning of May 5, 1930
ch07.note: The book here dates the congress to May 5–7, but on the preceding pages it quotes Zhang Wenqiu (May 20) and Hong Yangsheng without a date. The dates generally accepted in the scholarship are May 20–23, 1930. The sources genuinely disagree, and the account is left as the author gives it.

ch07.anchor: Even Lord Guan, he said, lost Maicheng
ch07.note: Two proverbial defeats from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms: Guan Yu (“Lord Guan”) was cornered and killed after the fall of Maicheng, and Zhuge Liang (“Kongming”) lost the strategic pass of Jieting through a subordinate’s blunder. To invoke them is to say that even the greatest commanders suffer a reverse.

ch07.anchor: along with Rou Shi, Feng Keng, and others
ch07.note: Rou Shi (1902–1931) and Feng Keng (1907–1931) were two of the “Five Martyrs of the League of Left-Wing Writers,” young writers arrested and secretly shot by the Kuomintang at Longhua, Shanghai, in February 1931. Lu Xun mourned them in his essay “In Memory of the Forgotten.” Hu Yepin was a third of the five.

The Long March (1934–1936) was the Red Army’s fighting retreat of some six thousand miles from its encircled base areas in the southeast to the far northwest, under constant Nationalist pursuit. The ordeal cost most of the marchers their lives, confirmed Mao Zedong as the Party’s paramount leader, and became the founding epic of Chinese Communism.

ch07.anchor: took part in the Revolution of 1911
ch07.note: The Revolution of 1911 (the Xinhai Revolution) overthrew the Qing dynasty and ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule, founding the Republic of China the following year. It opened with the Wuchang Uprising (see Chapter One).

Hongkou, the district north of Suzhou Creek, was the part of the International Settlement where the Japanese population and businesses concentrated; in practice it was Shanghai’s Japanese quarter, and Japanese-run premises there lay effectively beyond the reach of the Settlement’s own police.

ch07.anchor: changed into qipao and silk stockings and added gold and silver jewelry
ch07.note: The qipao (also known as the cheongsam), the close-fitting, high-collared one-piece dress that in 1930s Shanghai was the mark of a fashionable, modern woman.

Shou, the character for “long life,” is the emblem at the heart of a Chinese birthday celebration, hung large and gilded; the longevity peaches, long-life noodles, and Buddha’s-hand citrons set out around it all carry the same wish for the honoree’s long life.

A companion to the Lord Guan proverb just above, from the same Three Kingdoms lore: Zhuge Liang, styled Kongming, the age’s model strategist, lost the vital pass of Jieting after entrusting it to the overconfident Ma Su, and was forced into retreat. The sense: even a genius is not spared his defeats.

Daughter of Li Yimang, the Party veteran who fronted the congress’s cover “family” at the secret hospital. The author interviewed her at Beijing in March 2007, and her recollections of her father’s account frame much of this chapter.

Lin Yunan (1898–1931), a labor-movement leader and secretary-general of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions, ran the preparatory office for the congress; under the alias Li Jingtang he posed with Zhang Wenqiu as a returned-overseas-Chinese couple to hold the venue. He was executed by the Nationalists at Longhua, Shanghai, in February 1931.

Liu Qianchu (1897–1931), a Communist organizer and Zhang Wenqiu’s husband; by 1929 secretary of the CCP’s Shandong Provincial Committee. Arrested with her in 1929, he was executed by the Nationalists at Jinan in 1931.
An alias adopted by Zhang Wenqiu in 1929, when she became head of the women’s department of the CCP’s Shandong Provincial Committee.
A further alias taken by Zhang Wenqiu on her return to Shanghai in January 1930, under which she posed as Lin Yunan’s wife in the “home” that fronted the congress preparations.
The cover name under which Lin Yunan, got up as a wealthy returned overseas Chinese, posed as Zhang Wenqiu’s husband while setting up the congress office.
Another name for Liu Siqi, Zhang Wenqiu’s daughter, who later married Mao Zedong’s eldest son Mao Anying—the tie that makes Zhang, as the text says, “Mao Zedong’s kinswoman by marriage.”

The ruse identity given to Lin Yunan at the congress’s decoy “birthday hall,” where he figured as the son of “Old Master Zhao,” whose invented eightieth-birthday feast was the cover story every delegate had agreed to swear to.

A Party veteran freshly back from study in the Soviet Union (1928); at the congress he played the “younger brother” in Li Yimang’s cover family. He later became deputy head of the CCP’s International Liaison Department, as the text notes.

A cover name (also given as Li Kuntai) used at the congress by the future anti-Japanese martyr Zhao Yiman, who played the “younger sister” in Li Yimang’s cover family. Li Yimang learned her true identity only years later, on seeing the film Zhao Yiman.
The pet name of Zhao Yiman’s young son (Chen Yexian), to whom she addressed her farewell letter before her execution by the Japanese in 1936.

Zou Zhishu (born 1897, Jiaxing), an educated woman who joined the Party in 1926 and became a Central Special Branch operative; a First Section courier recruited by Zhou Enlai, she ran the catering at the secret “hospital.” She was later killed on the orders of the defector Gu Shunzhang.
Another name for Zou Zhishu.

ch07.anchor: Liu Ding at work on the edge of the secret hospital
ch07.note: Liu Ding (originally Kan Sijun, born 1902), deputy head of the Central Special Branch’s Second Section under Chen Geng; here he readied the delegates’ emergency escape route in rooms beside the “hospital.” He later served as the CCP’s secret representative to Zhang Xueliang’s Northeastern Army and played a part in the 1936 Xi’an Incident, and after 1949 became a leading figure in the PRC’s ordnance and machine-building industries.
The original name of Liu Ding (courtesy name Zunmin).

Liu Ding’s wife, a veteran of the Eighth Route Army and later an adviser at the Ministry of Ordnance Industry’s Intelligence Institute; she was the author’s chief source on Liu Ding’s Shanghai reconnaissance.

Sun Bingwen (1885–1927), an early Communist who, with Zhu De, sponsored Liu Ding’s entry into the Party while the three were in Germany in 1924. He was arrested and executed by the Nationalists in Shanghai in 1927.

Xiong Shihui’s No. 4 secret investigator, who was secretly Chen Geng’s mole; married to Zou Zhishu, who had brought him into the Party. His warning let the congress delegates withdraw before Xiong’s raid.
The original name of Song Zaisheng.

A Republican military figure from Zhuji, Zhejiang: a graduate of the Japanese Army Officers’ Academy (1904), a Tongmenghui member, and a participant in the 1911 Revolution who taught at the Baoding Military Academy. He was the teacher of both Xiong Shihui and Song Zaisheng—the tie that let the mole be placed at Xiong’s side.

He Changgong (1900–1987), a Red Army commander who had earlier helped bring Zhu De’s forces to join Mao Zedong at Jinggangshan. He attended the congress as a delegate from the Southeast Hubei base, where he was building the Fifth Red Army, and held senior Party and government posts after 1949.

Teng Daiyuan (1904–1974), a Red Army leader who with Peng Dehuai led the 1928 Pingjiang Uprising and founded the Fifth Red Army. A congress delegate, he gave a report of nearly 15,000 words for its Military Commission; after 1949 he became the first Minister of Railways of the People’s Republic.
Another name for Yu Haixia, delegate of the Daye Iron Mine workers, who traveled with He Changgong to the congress.
He Changgong’s wife, then still in Huarong; the Center offered to bring her to Shanghai with the surplus congress gold, an offer he firmly declined.

Xiao Ke (1907–2008), in 1930 chief of staff of the Fourth Red Army’s First Column, whose memoir supplies the account of the gold sent to the Center. One of the longest-lived senior commanders of the People’s Liberation Army, he was made a full general in 1955.

Party representative of the Fourth Red Army’s First Column, sent in 1930 to hand gold to the Center and so present at the congress as a Fourth Red Army delegate. He never rejoined the Red Army, being detained by the enemy at Xiamen and later studying at Fudan University and in Japan.

Son of the writers Hu Yepin and Ding Ling; a Soviet-trained shipbuilding engineer and a Shanghai neighbor of the author, whose recollection of his father’s guarded account of the congress the author quotes.
Jiang Zulin’s wife.
Jiang Zulin’s daughter, called Xiaoyan; a granddaughter of Hu Yepin and Ding Ling.

Zou Zhishu’s daughter, three years old when her mother was killed. Her given name Baosu puns on “protect the Soviet,” for the safeguarding of the congress. Given away as a child, she was traced again after 1949 through Zhou Enlai’s concern.
Zou Zhishu’s grandson (Song Baosu’s son), living in Shanghai, who asks only that his grandmother’s memory be left in peace.

Ai Siqi (1910–1966), a Marxist philosopher best known for popularizing Marxism in his Philosophy for the Masses; named here as one of the Party notables whose families lived at the Nanshagou compound in Beijing.

A prominent cinema on Bubbling Well Road in the International Settlement, opened in 1923 and renamed the Changjiang Theater in 1951; the congress was hidden in the crowded lanes just behind it, the busiest quarter being reckoned the safest cover.
A quiet, winding lane in the International Settlement (today Fengyang Road), running behind the Carlton Theater, where by several accounts the congress met.
A street in the International Settlement (today Huanghe Road); by Li Yimang’s account the congress venue stood at its junction with Burkill Road.
The present-day name of Hart Road, the International Settlement street that several early accounts give as the congress site.
A street in the International Settlement (today Taixing Road), cited here as a boundary of the Zhangjiazhai lanes.
A cluster of lanes off Avenue Road (near today’s Beijing West Road and Shimen No. 2 Road), site of a Party Center organ where Zou Zhishu did courier-cover work.

The creek that once marked the southern edge of the International Settlement, dividing it from the French Concession; filled in in 1915 to become a road (part of today’s Yan’an Road East). Its name became a byword for the pidgin—Yangjingbang English—spoken along it.
A residential compound for senior Party and state leaders in Beijing, where Li Yimang lived out his last years and where the author interviewed his daughter in 2007.

ch07.anchor: the All-China Federation of Trade Unions
ch07.note: The ACFTU (Zhonghua Quanguo Zong Gonghui), the CCP’s national trade-union body, founded in 1925. It lent its name as a co-sponsor of the congress, and its secretary-general, Lin Yunan, ran the preparations.

ch07.anchor: the League of Left-Wing Writers of China
ch07.note: The “Left League,” a Communist-led association of leftist writers founded in Shanghai in March 1930, with Lu Xun among its leading figures. Hu Yepin, Rou Shi, and Feng Keng attended the congress as its delegates.
The Shanghai Municipal Council (gongbuju), the foreign-run governing body of the International Settlement; even it, the passage notes, dared not touch the Japanese premises in Hongkou.

ch08.anchor: the seventeenth year of the Republic
ch08.note: The Republic of China numbered its years from its founding in 1912, so the seventeenth year of the Republic was 1928.

ch08.anchor: the Carnegie Institute of Technology in America he had read business management
ch08.note: The source writes Kangnaijie gongye daxue (康奈杰工业大学), given here as the Carnegie Institute of Technology, the engineering school in Pittsburgh (today part of Carnegie Mellon University). The two accounts in this passage disagree on what Xu Enzeng studied there: Zou Taofen recalls electrical engineering, Xu Enzeng’s own memoir business management.

ch08.anchor: classmate of Zou Taofen's the whole way
ch08.note: Zou Taofen (1895–1944), a celebrated progressive journalist and publisher, editor of Shenghuo (“Life”) Weekly and founder of the Life Bookstore, and one of the “Seven Gentlemen” jailed in 1936 for urging resistance to Japan. That the future head of the Kuomintang’s secret police had been his schoolmate, and then set agents to shadow him for years, is the irony the author is pointing to.

ch08.anchor: nor for her unbound natural feet
ch08.note: “Natural feet” (tianzu) meant feet never bound — a badge of the new, educated woman and of the movement against foot-binding, but still an oddity to an older generation. That Qian Zhuangfei’s mother disapproved of her son’s bride for her unbound feet places the family on the near side of a great social change.

Qian Xuantong (1887–1939), a leading philologist and iconoclast of the New Culture movement and a champion of the written vernacular. It was his prodding — the famous exchange about whether it was worth rousing the sleepers in a windowless “iron house” — that moved Lu Xun to write A Madman’s Diary (1918), the first Western-style story in vernacular Chinese, for the magazine New Youth.

ch08.anchor: the Wuyue kings Qian Liu and Qian Chu
ch08.note: Wuyue (907–978) was one of the kingdoms of the Five Dynasties period, centered on Hangzhou; Qian Liu was its founder and Qian Chu its last king, who yielded peacefully to the Song. The surname Qian (钱) is common in the region, and descent from its royal house a point of local pride.

ch08.anchor: the late film star Li Lili
ch08.note: Li Lili (1915–2005), born Qian Zhenzhen, a daughter of Qian Zhuangfei, was one of the brightest stars of 1930s Chinese cinema (Playthings, The Big Road, Daybreak); she took her stage surname from her mentor, the songwriter Li Jinhui. The album spoken of at the chapter’s close was her memoir in pictures.

The five classes of agent from the last chapter, “The Use of Spies,” of Sun Tzu’s Art of War: the local spy (a native of the enemy’s country), the inside spy (an enemy official suborned), the double or converted spy (the enemy’s agent turned back on him), the doomed or expendable spy (fed false information to carry to the enemy, at the cost of his life), and the surviving or living spy (who comes back with intelligence).

ch08.anchor: the 'Three Heroes of Longtan' are household names now
ch08.note: The “Three Heroes of Longtan” (龙潭三杰) — Qian Zhuangfei, Li Kenong, and Hu Di — are the three Communist agents who penetrated the Kuomintang’s intelligence service, the subject of this chapter. Longtan, “dragon’s pool,” echoes the set phrase longtan huxue, “the dragon’s pool and the tiger’s den” — the enemy’s innermost lair. The epithet is traditionally credited to Zhou Enlai.

ch08.anchor: to run the West Lake Exposition
ch08.note: The West Lake Exposition of 1929, held at Hangzhou over some four months, was one of Republican China’s largest national exhibitions, showcasing industry, agriculture, art, and education.

ch08.anchor: sending Nie Rongzhen to Gu Shunzhang's side
ch08.note: Nie Rongzhen (1899–1992), later one of the ten marshals of the People’s Republic; here he is moved into the Central Special Branch to keep the increasingly wayward Gu Shunzhang in check. His daughter Nie Li, quoted just below, became a lieutenant general and a leader of China’s defense-technology programs.

ch08.anchor: an attempt to assassinate Chiang Kai-shek
ch08.note: Whether Gu Shunzhang’s months of magic shows in Wuhan really screened a plot to kill Chiang Kai-shek is uncertain. The claim rests on the Kuomintang intelligence files used by Wakeman; the Communist sources quoted here treat the Wuhan sojourn rather as Gu’s self-indulgent dawdling. The author leaves the two readings standing side by side, as he found them.

ch08.anchor: the Central Plains War among Chiang
ch08.note: The Central Plains War (1930) was the largest of the warlord conflicts of the Nanjing decade, pitting Chiang Kai-shek against a coalition led by Yan Xishan, Feng Yuxiang, and Li Zongren. Chiang’s victory that autumn freed him to turn his armies on the Communist base areas — the campaigns that follow.

ch08.anchor: was the beginning of the First
ch08.note: The first of five “encirclement and suppression” campaigns (1930–1934) that Chiang Kai-shek mounted against the Central Soviet base in Jiangxi. The first four were beaten off; the fifth, in 1934, forced the Red Army out on the Long March. The Communists’ advance knowledge of the enemy’s plans, supplied by Qian Zhuangfei and his fellows, helped defeat the first two.

The four commanders on whose heads Chiang set a fifty-thousand-yuan bounty: Zhu De (1886–1976), commander-in-chief of the Red Army; Mao Zedong (1893–1976); Peng Dehuai (1898–1974); and Huang Gonglüe (1898–1931), a corps commander killed in action the next year. The source names them by surname alone, as the leaflet did.

Bang-bang chicken (bangbang ji) is a Sichuan cold dish of poached chicken torn into shreds under a spicy sesame dressing; the name is said to come from the wooden club once used to pound the meat tender.

ch08.anchor: the Horse King has three eyes
ch08.note: “The Horse King has three eyes” (Ma Wangye you san zhi yan) is a proverbial boast — roughly, “I’ll show him I’m not to be trifled with.” The Horse King, a folk deity, is shown with a third eye in his brow; to make a man “know” it is to make him feel one’s power.

Zeng Guofan (1811–1872), posthumously titled Zeng Wenzheng, was the Qing statesman and general who broke the Taiping Rebellion; his collected works stood on every literate household’s shelf. Keying a cipher to a widely owned book — a “book code” — gave sender and receiver a shared key that raised no suspicion.

The Wu (Wujiang), the great northern tributary of the Yangtze in Guizhou, crossed and recrossed by the Central Red Army during the Long March. Qian Zhuangfei died near it in the spring of 1935 — the death Zhou Enlai recalled at the Chongqing dinner with which this chapter opened.

How Qian Zhuangfei died is disputed. The older accounts have him killed by a local anti-Communist militia, or by bandits, after he was separated from the column during an air raid near Jinsha, Guizhou, on April 1, 1935; Wang Zhitao’s later suggestion, given here, that Chiang had him assassinated is a minority view resting on inference. What is not in doubt is that he was murdered — bound and stabbed — at about the age of forty, and that his body was found days afterward.

The Western Route Army was the Red Army force of some twenty thousand that crossed the Yellow River into the Gansu corridor in late 1936 and was all but destroyed by Muslim cavalry over the winter of 1936–37; the survivors straggled back to Yan’an. Ouyang Yi was among them.

ch08.anchor: His account is borne out by Meng Zhen
ch08.note: The block quotation is cited to a 1999 volume by Yang Yingqi and Zhang Wandong, which reprints the memoir of Zhang Guodong, the former Investigation Section trainee whose recollections the author leans on throughout this chapter; the author treats the quoted passage as Zhang Guodong's own account, and it is reproduced as printed.

The Eyuwan Soviet was a Communist rural base area on the borders of Hubei, Henan, and Anhui provinces, its name built from those provinces’ one-character abbreviations (E–Yu–Wan). A “Soviet” here means such a base — a revolutionary government on the Russian model — not the USSR.

“Li De” was the Chinese name of Otto Braun (1900–1974), the German Comintern military adviser to the Central Soviet, whose rigid, textbook tactics are widely blamed for the defeat that forced the Long March. Rendered as a Chinese name, he is easy to miss for a foreigner.

The Nanshe (“Southern Society”) was an influential literary society founded in 1909, its members largely revolutionary intellectuals hostile to the Qing. “Beiping” is the name Beijing carried from 1928 to 1949, while the national capital was at Nanjing.
Nanyang Public School (Nanyang College), founded in Shanghai in 1896, was one of China’s first modern institutions of higher learning and the forerunner of today’s Jiao Tong University.

ch08.anchor: broke his cauldrons and sank his boats
ch08.note: A classical idiom (po fu chen zhou): in 207 BC the warlord Xiang Yu, having crossed a river to give battle, sank his boats and smashed his cooking pots so that his soldiers knew there was no retreat and no meal but victory. To burn one’s bridges and stake everything on a single throw.

A set phrase (san jiao jiu liu, “the three teachings and the nine streams”): once the three doctrines — Confucian, Daoist, Buddhist — and the nine classical schools of thought, now every sort and station of people, high and low alike.

Zhang Xianzhong, younger brother of Zhang Zhenhua (Qian Zhuangfei’s wife) and an early member of the Chinese Communist Party. He was the family thread that drew Qian Zhuangfei and Hu Di into the Party: having brought his elder sister in in 1925, he in turn recruited his two brothers-in-law, Qian Zhuangfei and Hu Di, in 1926.

Sheng Yue (1907–2007), original name Sheng Zhongliang, one of the Moscow-trained “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks”; he studied at Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow and later served as secretary of the CCP Shanghai Central Bureau. After emigrating he wrote an English-language memoir, Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow and the Chinese Revolution, cited here as a source whose account of Gu Shunzhang’s arrest corroborates Cai Mengjian’s.

Li Lun (1927–2019), son of Li Kenong and younger brother of Li Li; he rose to lieutenant general in the People’s Liberation Army and served as deputy head of the General Logistics Department. He is quoted here recalling how his father, Qian Zhuangfei, and Hu Di were planted inside the Kuomintang secret service to feed intelligence back to the Party through Chen Geng and Zhou Enlai.

Wu Defeng (1896–1976), head of the CCP’s Central Communications Bureau, the body established in October 1930 to run the Party’s secret courier lines. In the chapter he directs the emergency repair of the shattered Yangtze courier network after Gu Shunzhang’s defection. After 1949 he became mayor of Wuhan and a vice-president of the Supreme People’s Court.

You Chongxin (original name You Wuhun), a Communist district secretary—former secretary of the West-Shanghai District Committee—who, after transfer to Wuhan, was arrested and turned traitor. Walking the streets of Hankou under Kuomintang guard to point out Communists, it was he who recognized Gu Shunzhang and cried out that he was the “commander-in-chief of the Shanghai rising,” bringing about Gu’s arrest on 24 April 1931.

He Chengjun (1882–1961), a senior Kuomintang general and governor of Hubei, concurrently director of the Wuhan field headquarters. His headquarters was where the captured Gu Shunzhang was held, and it was He Chengjun who—declining to see Gu himself—wired Nanjing to arrange Gu’s transfer to Chiang Kai-shek.

Wang Suqing, the “Miss Wang” who was Xu Enzeng’s kept mistress—originally the wife of a friend who had left her in Xu’s care while abroad. Qian Zhuangfei’s own family house sheltered her for Xu’s weekend trysts; it was Xu’s standing habit of leaving Nanjing every Saturday to visit her that left Qian alone with the telegrams reporting Gu Shunzhang’s defection.

Liu Qifu, Qian Zhuangfei’s son-in-law, husband of his daughter Qian Jiao. Qian sent him ahead to Shanghai to carry the first warning of Gu Shunzhang’s defection, but he could not reach Li Kenong before the appointed contact time and returned empty-handed.

Xu Shuangying, Qian Zhuangfei’s first wife, a Huzhou woman he married in 1914 and the mother of his daughters Qian Yeli and Qian Jiao. After Gu Shunzhang’s defection the Party sent word to both of Qian’s wives to go into hiding; by Li Kenong’s recollection she was then living on Chengdu Road in Shanghai.

Pan Hong (b. 1954), a prominent Chinese film and television actress. She wrote the preface to the 2001 photo album assembled by Qian Zhuangfei’s daughter Li Lili, the pioneering 1930s screen star whose recollections are drawn on throughout this chapter.

Gu Zhuxuan (1885–1956), a Green Gang boss known as the “tycoon of Jiangbei” and proprietor of Shanghai’s Tianchan Stage, a leading opera theater. The anecdote marks out the gangland world Gu Shunzhang moved in: asked to settle Gu Zhuxuan’s quarrel with a rival theater owner, Gu Shunzhang led his men and beat the rival to death.

Gan Naiguang (1897–1956), a Kuomintang politician and economist and one of the leading members of the Reorganizationist faction headed by Wang Jingwei. He is named here among that faction whose challenge to Chiang Kai-shek helped prompt the creation of the Investigation Section, forerunner of the “Zhongtong” secret service.

The Zhengyuan Industrial Company was the cover name for Xu Enzeng’s Nanjing secret-service organ—the innocuous signboard hung over the door of the Investigation Section’s building near the Central Hotel on Zhongshan East Road. Qian Zhuangfei worked there as Xu’s confidential secretary, and it was here that the captured Gu Shunzhang was later brought and won over.

The Yangtze News Agency, the Nanjing controlling organ operating under the Zhengyuan Industrial Company’s cover, which Qian Zhuangfei directed alongside his post as Xu Enzeng’s confidential secretary. Its office in the Central Hotel was one of the listening posts Qian shut down—slashing a cross on its wall map as the signal to break contact and withdraw—before he fled to warn the Party.

The Great Wall News Agency was the Tianjin news organ headed by Hu Di under Investigation Section cover. It formed the northern point of Xu Enzeng’s intended anti-Communist “iron triangle” of Shanghai, Nanjing, and Tianjin—which in truth operated as three Communist agents lodged inside the enemy’s own apparatus.

The CCP Shanghai Central Bureau was the Party’s leading organ in Shanghai after the Central Committee relocated to the soviet base areas, coordinating the remaining underground work in the Kuomintang-held cities. Sheng Yue, cited here, served as its secretary.

ch09.anchor: then chairman of the CCP Central Politburo and of its Standing Committee
ch09.note: Xiang Zhongfa (1880–1931), the man this chapter is about. A Wuhan dockworker and boatman turned union organizer, he was raised up at the Party’s 1928 Sixth Congress to nominal head of the Party, a proletarian figurehead; real authority lay with Li Lisan, and then with the Moscow-backed Wang Ming group and the Comintern. Gu Shunzhang’s defection in April 1931 exposed him, and he was seized in Shanghai on June 22, 1931, and shot within days. Whether he broke under interrogation is the question the chapter weighs. The standard accounts, and the Party’s own later verdict (Deng Yingchao, 1988, endorsed by Chen Yun), hold that he confessed at once and gave up his comrades; a dissenting minority (Zhang Ji’en) argued the confession was a forgery. His arrest and execution are not in doubt; what the sources here contest is the extent of his betrayal.

ch09.anchor: Huang Mulan has told us a story
ch09.note: Huang Mulan (1907–2017), an underground Communist courier and liaison in early-1930s Shanghai, later a businesswoman in Hong Kong and, after 1949, a prisoner for many years before her rehabilitation. Her long life and her 2012 memoir made her a celebrated figure, marketed as the “most beautiful red agent.” Her account of Xiang Zhongfa’s capture — that she overheard it by chance in a café — is the version the author sets out to test in this chapter, and treats throughout as an interested, self-flattering source. Her portrait appears below.

ch09.anchor: saving of Zhou Enlai and Guan Xiangying
ch09.note: Guan Xiangying (1902–1946), a Manchu Communist and youth and labor organizer, later political commissar of the 120th Division of the Eighth Route Army. Here he is simply the imprisoned comrade Huang Mulan was tasked with helping to free.

ch09.anchor: a film at the Grand
ch09.note: The Grand Theater (Da Guangming), a landmark cinema on Bubbling Well Road; its Art Deco building, remodeled in 1933 by the architect László Hudec, was among the grandest picture houses in East Asia.

ch09.anchor: a heroine in the mold of Hua Mulan
ch09.note: Hua Mulan, the legendary woman warrior of the old Ballad of Mulan, who disguised herself as a man to take her aged father’s place in the army. Huang Mulan’s given name, Mulan (慕兰, “admiring Mulan”), is drawn from her — the point of the wordplay in this passage.

ch09.anchor: as for *Dream of the Red Chamber*
ch09.note: Two of the great classical Chinese novels: Romance of the Three Kingdoms, a sweeping historical war epic, and Dream of the Red Chamber, an intimate novel of a declining gentry house and its doomed romance. Huang Mulan offers her taste for the martial epic over the domestic romance as proof of her “masculine” temper.

ch09.anchor: publicly announced by Dong Biwu
ch09.note: Dong Biwu (1886–1975), a founder of the Chinese Communist Party and a delegate to its First Congress in 1921; after 1949 he became a vice-chairman of the People’s Republic and, for a time, its acting head of state.

ch09.anchor: married Wan Xiyan
ch09.note: Wan Xiyan (1900–1928), a Communist organizer and propagandist, Huang Mulan’s second husband; he was killed in 1928 leading a peasant force against the town of Wan’an in Jiangxi.

ch09.anchor: was He Chang, a member of the Sixth Central Committee
ch09.note: He Chang (1906–1935), a Communist labor and military-political leader, Huang Mulan’s third husband; he died during the Long March.

ch09.anchor: Chen Zhigao invited me for coffee
ch09.note: Chen Zhigao, a Shanghai lawyer and the son of a judge of the Mixed Court, who used his father’s name and his own connections to win the release of arrested comrades, and who later married Huang Mulan.

ch09.anchor: a student at Aurora University in Shanghai
ch09.note: The Université l’Aurore (Zhendan), a French Jesuit university in Shanghai’s French Concession, known for its law and medical faculties.

ch09.anchor: the North China Political Security Bureau
ch09.note: The Communist clandestine security and counter-intelligence network in the Beiping–Tianjin region, set up by Chen Geng after the Shanghai apparatus was blown. (Beiping was the name of Beijing from 1928 to 1949.)

ch09.anchor: the "Moskvin" of the Comintern department's report
ch09.note: “Moskvin” was Zhou Enlai’s codename in his dealings with the Comintern; the report’s reference to “Comrade Mo(skvin)” directing the reorganized special-work apparatus is thus a veiled naming of Zhou himself.

ch09.anchor: the Metropole Hotel and lie low for a time
ch09.note: The Metropole Hotel (Ducheng Fandian), a foreign-run hotel; the leaders’ brazen arrival in business dress, as the account has it, was itself the cover.

ch09.anchor: No. 44 Yong'anli on North Sichuan Road
ch09.note: A shikumen lane house in Hongkou used as one of Zhou Enlai’s Shanghai safe houses, now preserved as a memorial to his underground years. The author cites its later designation to press his point that Zhou would not still have been living there sixteen hours after Xiang’s arrest.

ch09.anchor: through Bao Wenwei, Wu Xingya
ch09.note: Bao Wenwei (1902–1991), a scholar of French literature who, under Special Branch direction, penetrated the Songhu Garrison Command as its French interpreter; he later became a university professor and the Chinese translator of Rabelais. His family’s account and Pan Hannian’s differ on the dates of his service, a discrepancy the author probes at length here.

ch09.anchor: his mother He Xiangning
ch09.note: He Xiangning (1878–1972), a revolutionary, painter, and widow of the Nationalist leader Liao Zhongkai; her son Liao Chengzhi (1908–1983), a Communist jailed at various times by both sides, rose after 1949 to senior posts in overseas-Chinese and foreign affairs.

ch09.anchor: the Hanyeping Company's ship No. 180
ch09.note: The Han-Ye-Ping Coal and Iron Company — the Hanyang ironworks, the Daye iron mines, and the Pingxiang colliery combined — was China’s first large modern iron-and-steel enterprise, centered on the Wuhan region where Xiang Zhongfa began as a worker.

ch09.anchor: the great Jinghan Railway workers' strike
ch09.note: The February 1923 strike on the Beijing–Hankou (Jinghan) Railway, crushed by the warlord Wu Peifu in the “February Seventh Massacre,” was a landmark and a bloody defeat for the early Communist-led labor movement.

ch09.anchor: Luo Zhanglong describes the Sixth Congress
ch09.note: Luo Zhanglong (1896–1995), one of the earliest Communist labor leaders; he broke with the leadership over the Fourth Plenum of 1931 and was expelled, which colors his memoir of these years.

ch09.anchor: Mif took his place
ch09.note: Pavel Mif, a Comintern official and rector of Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow, was the patron of Wang Ming and the Moscow-trained “Returned Students” (the “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks”). Luo Zhanglong’s account shows him installing Xiang Zhongfa as Party Secretary on Stalin’s instructions, to visibly muted applause.

ch09.anchor: those stood for the two most fashionable cuts
ch09.note: The joke turns on the shop-sign words Su-Guang-Cheng: Su for Suzhou, Guang for Guangdong (Canton), chengyi for ready-made clothes. “Suguangcheng” is not one shop’s name but the generic label “Suzhou-and-Cantonese tailoring,” so it hangs on more signboards than any other — which is also why the sources cannot agree whether Xiang’s safe house was the Suguangcheng grain shop or the Suguangcheng tailor shop.

ch09.anchor: Yang Hu, to negotiate
ch09.note: Yang Hu (1889–1966), a Green Gang-connected Nationalist general and Shanghai garrison commander, a principal enforcer of Chiang Kai-shek’s April 1927 purge of the Communists in the city.

ch09.anchor: then at Mount Lu, received the first urgent telegram
ch09.note: Mount Lu (Lushan) in Jiangxi, a cool highland resort that served as Chiang Kai-shek’s summer headquarters; from here he directed the Encirclement campaigns against the Communist base areas.

ch09.anchor: Kuomintang Zhongtong publication *The Turn* carries
ch09.note: The Turn (Zhuanbian) was an internal Zhongtong compilation of recantations by Communist defectors. The “Report of the Former Bogus CCP General Secretary Xiang Zhongfa” in its appendix — his so-called Confession — is the disputed document at the center of this chapter’s argument.

ch09.anchor: the Youth League General Secretary Qin Bangxian
ch09.note: Qin Bangxian (1907–1946), better known as Bo Gu, one of the Moscow-trained “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks”; within months he would head the Party’s Provisional Center.

ch09.anchor: Volume Eleven of the *Shilüe Gaoben*
ch09.note: The Shilüe Gaoben (Draft Chronicle) is the vast day-by-day compilation drawn from Chiang Kai-shek’s papers and diaries. The author’s discovery there of Chiang’s June 23 telegram ordering Xiang Zhongfa shot is the chapter’s clinching evidence: the “secret cable” whose very existence the section title disputes did, corroborated in Chiang’s own record, exist.

ch09.anchor: Li Dezhao
ch09.note: Li Dezhao, secretary-general of the Party’s Shanghai Central Bureau, arrested by the authorities in 1934.

ch09.anchor: Xujiahui Cathedral
ch09.note: The Xujiahui Cathedral (in the older romanization Zikawei or Sicawei), St. Ignatius, the great neo-Gothic Jesuit church in the southwest of Shanghai and the center of the Catholic mission that had stood at Xujiahui since the seventeenth century.

ch10.anchor: a cold wind and a bitter rain
ch10.note: The chapter opens on a four-part play on the Chinese figures that pair wind with rain. Chen Duxiu’s years were hufeng-huanyu, “summoning wind and rain,” commanding events at will; Qu Qiubai’s brief tenure a “violent storm”; Xiang Zhongfa’s a “foul wind and bloody rain,” a reign of terror; and Bo Gu’s a qifeng-kuyu, a “cold wind and bitter rain,” the set phrase for wretched, comfortless times.

Ruijin, a town in southern Jiangxi, was the seat of the Central Revolutionary Base, or Central Soviet — the largest of the Communist rural bases and, from November 1931, capital of the self-proclaimed Chinese Soviet Republic. It was the destination of the underground courier lines this chapter describes, and the starting point, in 1934, of the Long March.

Zhang Wentian (1900–1976), who wrote under the name Luo Fu, one of the Moscow-trained “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks.” He took over as the Party’s general secretary in early 1935, after the Zunyi conference, and later served as a diplomat and vice foreign minister.
Qin Guan (1049–1100), styled Shaoyou, a major lyric (ci) poet of the Northern Song and one of the disciples gathered around Su Shi. The line of descent is the Qin family’s own claim.

Qin Jin (1467–1544), styled Fengshan, a high official under the Ming Jiajing emperor. The family phrase renders his career: he headed five of the boards across the Ming’s two capitals, Beijing and Nanjing (each kept a parallel set of Six Boards), and rose to the honorary rank of Grand Guardian (taibao). The Jichang Garden his family laid out survives in Wuxi as one of the country’s celebrated classical gardens.
Qin Jiacong (English name Frank Ching), a journalist and a descendant of the same Wuxi Qin line, whose family history traces the clan across some nine centuries.

An echo of the May Fourth attack on Confucian ritualism — the “rites that eat people” of Lu Xun’s Diary of a Madman (1918). Bo Gu, writing here as “Shanglin” in 1925, was a student caught up in that iconoclasm.

ch10.anchor: bleak and forlorn and steeped in grief
ch10.note: The phrase is Li Qingzhao’s, the opening reduplicatives of her famous song lyric “Note After Note” (Sheng sheng man) — a byword in Chinese for desolate grief.

“Changlin” is Bo Gu, whom his mother knew by his childhood name; the memoirist Qin Moya is his eldest daughter. Bo Gu died on April 8, 1946, in the air crash at Heicha Mountain in Xingxian, Shanxi, that killed a group of Party leaders returning from the Chongqing talks — the “April 8 martyrs.” His mother, kept in the dark, went on waiting for him.

Huarun, in English China Resources, grew out of the Party’s underground trading network described in this chapter; today it is a state-owned conglomerate among the Fortune Global 500. Qin Bangli (1908–1968), Bo Gu’s younger brother, ran it under the alias Yang Lin; the chapter follows him from a Wuxi money house to the founding of the firm.

The Sino-French Drugstore (Zhongfa Yaofang) was a well-known Western-style pharmacy chain in Republican Shanghai; a branch in the treaty port of Shantou, in eastern Guangdong, gave the Party a respectable commercial front and a waystation on the sea route south.

ch10.anchor: escorted several hundred comrades in all through enemy-held territory
ch10.note: The names that follow are a roll-call of the men who would run the People’s Republic — among them Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Liu Shaoqi, and Hu Yaobang, and the future marshals Ye Jianying, Liu Bocheng, and Nie Rongzhen — passed one by one along this single courier line into the Jiangxi base.

ch10.anchor: took the train on to Shaoyang
ch10.note: Shaoyang is in central Hunan, far off this Guangdong-to-Fujian route; the name as printed in the Biography of Chen Yun is almost certainly a slip, most likely for a place near Shantou. —Trans.

ch10.anchor: chief of the executive section of the Central Political Security Bureau
ch10.note: The Central Political Security Bureau, formed in 1931, was the security and counter-intelligence organ of the Jiangxi Soviet — a separate body from the Shanghai Special Branch, and a forerunner of the Party’s later state-security apparatus. It ran its own courier lines, which is the crux of the author’s argument here: the “Chen Pannian” of these accounts belongs to it and is not the famous Pan Hannian.

ch10.anchor: good at building a new one
ch10.note: Both slogans are Mao Zedong’s, from 1949. The first paraphrases “Farewell, Leighton Stuart” (August 1949), whose received text reads “Blockade us for eight or ten years and all of China’s problems will be solved”; the book gives “decades.” The second is from his opening address to the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference in September 1949, on the eve of the People’s Republic.

Qin Hong (born 1967), a granddaughter of Bo Gu (through his second son, Qin Gang) and a 1990 graduate of the School of Economics at Peking University. Her 2014 study Huarun: A Miniature of Modern History traces the origins of China Resources, and this chapter draws on it and on her family reminiscences throughout.

Lu Futan (1891–1969), a native of Tai’an, Shandong, and by 1931 a veteran labor organizer. He was one of the three Standing Committee members of the Provisional Central Politburo formed in Shanghai in September 1931. Arrested in the Shanghai concessions in early 1933, he defected and served the Nationalists’ Central Statistics Bureau (the Zhongtong); imprisoned by the Communists after 1949, he was executed in 1969, the only former Politburo Standing Committee member the Party has put to death.

Li Zhusheng (1903–1973), from Shouxian in Anhui, a Politburo member of the 1931 Provisional Center and secretary of the Party’s Shanghai Central Bureau. Arrested in June 1934, he was turned by Xu Enzeng and gave up his colleagues; he later joined the Nationalist intelligence apparatus, was imprisoned again after 1949, and died in prison in 1973.

A qianzhuang, or native bank — a traditional Chinese private banking house dealing in deposits, loans, and the exchange of the many silver and copper currencies then in circulation. Qin Bangli apprenticed at the Fuyuan house in Wuxi from the age of fourteen, and the head for figures he trained there served the Party’s clandestine trade for the rest of his life.

Qin Qi (1907–1927), an early Wuxi Communist and labor leader who became chairman of the Wuxi General Trade Union in January 1927. He led the local money-trade and textile workers and was seized and secretly killed by Nationalist forces in April 1927, at the age of twenty, during the crushing of the labor movement; Qin Bangli had served under him on the money-trade union’s executive.

Liu Qunxian (born 1907), a Wuxi textile worker who rose to become a leading woman labor organizer; Edgar Snow called her an outstanding Chinese woman worker’s leader. She studied at the Communist University of the Toilers of the East in Moscow, where she married Bo Gu in 1928, and headed the women workers’ department of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions. She led the women’s company on the Long March, went to the Soviet Union for medical treatment in 1939, and is believed to have died there during the Second World War.

Qi Yuande, wife of Wu Defeng, then head of the Party’s Central Communications Bureau. Her memoir of the Shanghai underground years, quoted at length here, is used by the author to correct the romantic legend of specially made furniture with false compartments and to show how the furniture shops actually served the network.
Hongmiao (“Red Temple”), a locality in Shanghai where, according to the Biography of Chen Yun, the Party ran a secondhand furniture-and-woodware shop as one of its commercial fronts.
Qin Fuquan, the eldest son of Qin Bangli (Yang Lin), whose 2007 reminiscences are a source for the six Shanghai shops his father ran as underground communications stations.

Lu Weiliang, once head of the Dabu courier station on the secret Shanghai–Central Soviet route through eastern Guangdong and western Fujian, and later deputy chief procurator of the Guangdong Provincial People’s Procuratorate. His 1980 recollections supply the itinerary and the long roster of leaders his station escorted through enemy territory.

One of the many comrades Lu Weiliang recalled the Dabu station having escorted between 1930 and 1932. As with several lesser names on his list, the person behind this recalled reading cannot be securely identified, and the romanization is provisional.
A name on the roster of those Lu Weiliang recalled the Dabu station escorting; the individual cannot be securely identified from the memoir alone, and the reading is given as printed.
Another of the comrades in Lu Weiliang’s recalled roster of those escorted through enemy-held territory; an obscure figure whose identity the memoir does not fix.
One more name in Lu Weiliang’s roster of escorted comrades, listed as traveling with his wife; the reading follows the memoir as printed and the person is not otherwise securely identified here.

Zhuo Xiong (1915–2009), chief of the executive section of the Party’s State (Central) Political Security Bureau, charged with guarding the central leaders. He escorted Bo Gu, Chen Yun, and later the Comintern adviser Otto Braun into the Central Soviet, drawing off Nationalist troops to see them through. After 1949 he held senior posts, including vice-minister of geology and of civil affairs.

A stop named in the itinerary given by the Biography of Chen Yun for the 1933 journey from Shantou toward the Soviet area; the author flags the whole route in that account (including “Shaoyang”) as garbled, and the reading of this place name is provisional.
Co-author, with Li Zhiying, of A Biography of Qin Bangxian (Bo Gu) (2007), one of the scholarly lives of Bo Gu the author weighs here against the Biography of Chen Yun and other sources.
Co-author, with Wu Baopu, of A Biography of Qin Bangxian (Bo Gu) (2007), cited here for its account of the 1933 escape route from Shanghai to western Fujian.

Co-author, with Li Shuting, of the 2003 account of the Party’s sea courier line, based on an interview with Zhuo Xiong; the author uses it to argue that the escort “Chen Pannian” has been wrongly conflated with the intelligence officer Pan Hannian.
Co-author, with Sun Junting, of the 2003 interview-based account of the Shanghai–Hong Kong–Shantou sea courier line built by the communications section of the Central Political Security Bureau.
A principal thoroughfare in Central, on Hong Kong Island, named after Sir George William Des Voeux, governor of Hong Kong from 1887 to 1891. Qin Bangli’s postwar trading firm took an office here.
An office building in Central, Hong Kong (its Chinese name, Taizihang, the “Prince’s Firm”), which housed the Hongkong Telephone Company; the Lianhe Company rented its office here in 1946.

The Tianlonghang, a trading firm Qin Bangli registered in Hong Kong with a branch in Guangzhou, run in tandem with the Lianhe Company so that trade between Hong Kong and the mainland could be conducted through firms at both ends.
Huang Meixian, an accountant at the firm, who supplied the English name “China Resources” for Huarun — a rendering approved, the text notes, by the Red Army commander-in-chief Zhu De.
Qin Gang, the second son of Bo Gu (Qin Bangxian) and the father of Qin Hong, whose writings on China Resources this chapter draws upon.

The Lianhehang (“Union Firm”), the Hong Kong trading company Qin Bangli founded and the direct forerunner of China Resources. Renamed the Lianhe Import and Export Company in 1946 and rechristened Huarun at Christmas 1947, it grew from an underground communications front into a state enterprise later ranked among the Fortune Global 500.

The cover name Qin Bangli used on first coming to Hong Kong. In the Wuxi dialect “Lian’an” is a homophone of lianhe, “union,” and the author notes that the firm he founded, the Lianhehang, was in effect named after this alias; he also worked under the name Yang Lin.

ch11.note: The Seventy-Two Tenants (Qishi’er jia fangke) is a classic Shanghai huaji comedy, a stage farce, later filmed, about the crowd of tenants packed into one ramshackle lane house, famous for its gallery of city types. The words filling this paragraph — niangyi, afei, biesan, baixiangren and the rest — are Shanghai and Wu-dialect street slang; the author lays them on to fix xiaokai in the same idiom of the 1930s city.

ch11.anchor: his early novel The Bitter Cup
ch11.note: The Bitter Cup (Kubei) was an early novel by Pan Hannian, who first made his name in Shanghai as a left-wing writer and editor before he turned to underground work. The scare-quoted phrases here are the novel’s own romantic-decadent language, which the author quotes with a dry smile.

The Zhongshan suit (after Sun Yat-sen, whose Chinese name was Sun Zhongshan; known in the West as the “Mao suit”) was the plain, semi-military tunic adopted by Chinese revolutionaries and later worn by the Republic’s officials. Because the Kuomintang left and the Communists favored it, wearing one could get a man branded “red.”

The “Left League” is the League of Left-Wing Writers (see the note at Chapter Seven); the “Dramatists’ League” is its sister body, the League of Left-Wing Dramatists. Both were Communist-led cultural fronts of the early 1930s, and Pan Hannian’s Party work in this period ran through them.

ch11.anchor: little Elisa, in The Wild Swans
ch11.note: Hans Christian Andersen’s tale The Wild Swans gives the chapter its title. Its heroine, Elisa, can free her eleven brothers — turned into swans by their stepmother the queen — only by weaving them shirts of nettles, and she may not speak a word until the task is done, on pain of their deaths. Her enforced silence is the author’s figure for the underground worker who can tell no one what he does.

The “CC Clique” was the Kuomintang faction built around the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, which controlled the party’s organization apparatus and, through the Zhongtong (see the note at Chapter One), much of its secret-police and anti-Communist work.

ch11.anchor: Xu Minghong for the Nineteenth Route Army
ch11.note: Xu Minghong (1897–1934) was the Nineteenth Route Army’s secretary-general and a secret Communist, and it was he who negotiated the army’s anti-Japanese accords with Pan Hannian. After the Fujian revolt collapsed he was captured and executed by the Kuomintang in 1934 — the death Liang Shuming mourns below.

The China Weekly Review (Chinese Milei-shi Pinglun-bao, after its American founder Thomas Millard) was Shanghai’s leading English-language weekly, an influential voice on Chinese affairs from 1917 into the 1950s.

ch11.anchor: to resist the outside one must first pacify within
